title: One Honest Prophet, One King's Death
overview: Against four hundred agreeable prophets, one man warns King Ahab that his war will cost him his life, and it does.

parts.label: A war plan (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: Ahab, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, wants to win back Ramoth Gilead, a town east of the Jordan River held by Aram (roughly modern Syria), and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah to the south, agrees to join him. Jehoshaphat insists on asking the LORD first, and when four hundred court prophets all say yes, he asks for another voice, so Ahab grudgingly sends for Micaiah, a prophet he hates for always bringing bad news.

parts.label: Pressure to agree (vv. 10-14)
parts.note: The two kings sit in state at the city gate while Zedekiah, one of the court prophets, waves iron horns, an old picture of strength, to act out Aram being gored. A messenger urges Micaiah to fall in line, but he says he will speak only what the LORD tells him.

parts.label: Micaiah's two visions (vv. 15-23)
parts.note: Micaiah first echoes the others, apparently in mockery, then describes Israel scattered like sheep with no shepherd, meaning the king will die and the army will go home. He then pictures God as a king consulting his court, where a spirit offers to mislead Ahab through his prophets, a startling image that readers have long struggled to explain.

parts.label: Slapped and jailed (vv. 24-28)
parts.note: Zedekiah hits Micaiah and sneers at the idea that God's spirit left him to speak through Micaiah instead. Ahab orders Micaiah kept on bare prison rations until he returns safely, and Micaiah replies that if Ahab comes back alive, then the LORD did not speak through him.

parts.label: Ahab dies in battle (vv. 29-40)
parts.note: Ahab goes into battle in disguise while Jehoshaphat wears royal robes, and the enemy charioteers, ordered to target only Ahab, chase Jehoshaphat until they see their mistake. An arrow shot at random finds a gap in Ahab's armor, he bleeds to death in his chariot by evening, and dogs lick his blood in Samaria, which the writer ties to an earlier warning from the prophet Elijah.

parts.label: Two more reigns (vv. 41-53)
parts.note: Jehoshaphat is judged a good king, though the local hilltop shrines called high places stayed in use, and his trading ships bound for Ophir, a source of gold whose location is uncertain, were wrecked before they sailed. Ahab's son Ahaziah rules Israel only two years and follows his parents in worshiping Baal, a Canaanite god.

disagreement: Christians differ over what Micaiah's vision of a misleading spirit means: some take it as God actively sending deception as judgment, while others read it as a vivid picture of God allowing Ahab the self-deception he already wanted, noting that Micaiah's warning still told him the truth.
think: When nearly everyone around you agrees, what makes it hard to take seriously the one voice saying what you do not want to hear?
